title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
description: Brute force to optimized: comparing against every stored word directly versus a trie with DFS wildcard search.

content.title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Design a data structure supporting addWord(word), which adds a word, and search(word), which returns true if there is any previously added word that matches, where the search word may contain "." characters that match any single letter.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["addWord(word)","Inserts word into the structure"],["search(word)","Returns true if some added word matches, treating \".\" as a wildcard for any single character"],["Goal","Support both operations efficiently using a trie plus DFS for wildcard matching"],["Constraints","Up to 10^4 total addWord calls, words up to 25 characters"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Add a word\" then \"search with exact or wildcard characters\"","A standard trie for storage, with DFS/backtracking for search to handle the wildcard branching"],["\".\" matches any single character","When a wildcard is hit during the trie walk, recursively try every child instead of just one"]]}

blocks.text: addWord behaves exactly like a normal trie insert. search behaves like a normal trie walk EXCEPT whenever a "." is encountered, the search must try every child at that trie node (via recursion), returning true if any of those branches eventually leads to a complete match.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking a Filled Crossword Blank Against Every Possible Letter
blocks.text: Picture searching a dictionary trie for a word where some letters are blanked out. At every blank, every possible letter branch must be tried, continuing the search down each branch to see if any leads to a complete valid word.

blocks.caption: When "." is encountered during search, DFS branches into every child at that level

blocks.text: Before comparing the search word against every stored word individually, notice that a trie already shares common prefixes across stored words, and a wildcard character just means "branch into every child here" rather than following one fixed path.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: addWord is a completely standard trie insertion, no different from any other trie problem.

Observation 2: search walks the trie one character at a time, following the matching child exactly as usual, UNLESS the current search character is ".".

Observation 3: On ".", instead of following one specific child, recursively try EVERY child of the current node, and succeed if ANY of those recursive attempts succeeds.

Observation 4: The recursion bottoms out successfully only when the full search word has been consumed AND the current trie node is marked as an end-of-word.
This leads to a standard trie for storage, with a recursive DFS search function that branches into every child whenever the search word has a "." at the current position.
Store every added word in a plain list. For search, compare the search word against every stored word directly, character by character, treating "." as matching anything.
Why the code is written this way

items: Comparing against every stored word directly implements the definition simply.
This wastes time re-checking similar prefixes across many stored words, something a trie naturally shares.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(number of words times word length) per search.
Space: O(total characters stored).
Limitation: a trie plus DFS search shares common prefixes across all stored words and only branches (rather than fully restarting) at wildcard positions.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Store words in a trie, exactly as usual for addWord. For search, write a recursive DFS function taking the current trie node and current search position. If the current search character is a normal letter, follow that one child (or fail if absent). If it is ".", recursively try every child of the current node. Succeed at the end of the recursion only if the search word is fully consumed and the current node is marked end-of-word.
Use a standard trie for storage; search via DFS that follows one child normally, or branches into all children at a wildcard.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Position","Character","Action"],"rows":[["0",".","Branch into every child of root: b, d, m"],["1 (via b)","a","Follow child a"],["2 (via b-a)","d","Follow child d, reaches end of word: MATCH found, return true"]]}

blocks.text: The trie shares common prefixes across all added words automatically, so a normal character follows exactly one path just like a plain trie search. A wildcard character simply means "try every branch here," and since the recursion only reports success at a true end-of-word after consuming the entire search word, every possible combination of concrete letters standing in for the wildcards is implicitly explored without ever materializing them.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(26 raised to the number of wildcards times word length) worst case per search, O(word length) with no wildcards.
Space: O(total characters stored).

blocks.text: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure is the canonical trie-plus-wildcard-DFS problem: normal trie insertion, and a recursive search that branches at every wildcard.

items: Forgetting to check node.isEnd (not just that the recursion reached the end of the search word) at the base case.
Iterating a trie node's children incorrectly, or forgetting to return true as soon as ANY branch under a wildcard succeeds.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "a wildcard means try every child recursively, a normal character means follow exactly one child" clarifies the core recursive structure immediately.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "support a wildcard character matching any single letter during search", think: trie plus DFS that branches into every child at a wildcard position.

items: How would you support a wildcard that matches any SEQUENCE of characters (like "*"), not just a single character?
Implement Trie and Word Search II, other trie-plus-DFS problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The list-comparison approach costs O(number of words times length) per search; the trie-plus-DFS approach costs O(word length) with no wildcards, degrading only with the number of wildcard characters present, the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: trie for storage, DFS with branching for wildcard search.
Core Idea: a normal character follows exactly one trie child; a wildcard recursively tries every child.
Time: O(number of words times length) per search for the brute force, O(word length) typical (worse with many wildcards) for the trie approach.
Most Important Observation: a wildcard is simply "branch into every child here," implemented via straightforward recursion.
Interview Difficulty: a standard, frequently asked trie-plus-DFS design problem.
One line memory trick: normal trie insert, DFS search that branches on dot.
